| **Type** | framework — Dynan, Elmendorf & Sheiner — Fiscal Policy and the Rise of AI |
| **Source** | <https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/202608_DynanElmendorfSheiner.pdf> |
| **Tags** | Mild AUG, Strong CONC (top quintile) |
| **Policy stance** | off |
| **Likelihood** | plausible — Early AI gains are going mainly to leading firms, capital and high earners, though a half-point productivity boost sustained for 30 years is not yet visible in the data. |
| **Assessed** | 2026-11-27 |

AI lifts US productivity growth by half a point a year but all the extra labour and capital income goes to the top fifth. Because that income is taxed at higher rates, federal debt falls further than under shared gains, while inequality rises sharply.

## Social contract scores (draft)

| Promise | Score | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hard work pays | 3 | No jobs are lost, but all extra labour income goes to the top quintile, so effort pays no more than without AI for the other four fifths. |
| Affordable essentials |  | Not addressed: the extract lists housing, health-insurance and care options but says nothing about prices in the scenario. |
| Reliable safety net | 3 | The existing tax and transfer system redistributes automatically, keeping more people eligible for Medicaid and CHIP than under shared gains, with no displacement to test it. |
| Responsive government | 3 | The budget improves more than under shared gains and policymakers keep the choice over progressivity, but the sizeable rise in inequality carries the authors' named risk of disproportionate political power. |
| Time for what matters |  | Not addressed: nothing in the extract bears on family, community or free time in this scenario. |
